deck.name: AP Environmental Science
deck.description: Study ecosystems, biodiversity, populations, Earth systems, resource use, pollution, energy, and global environmental change through AP-aligned practice questions.

questions.prompt: A marsh contains reeds, fish, bacteria, water, and dissolved oxygen. Which listed component is abiotic?
choices: Dissolved oxygen
Decomposer bacteria
Small fish
Rooted reeds
questions.explanation: Abiotic factors are nonliving physical or chemical parts of an ecosystem. Dissolved oxygen is a chemical condition; the other listed components are organisms.

questions.prompt: A meadow fixes 2,400 g C/m²/year by photosynthesis and producers use 900 g C/m²/year in respiration. What is its net primary productivity?
choices: 1,500 g C/m²/year
2,400 g C/m²/year
3,300 g C/m²/year
0.375 g C/m²/year
questions.explanation: NPP = GPP − respiration = 2,400 − 900 = 1,500 g C/m²/year. NPP is the energy or carbon stored as producer biomass and available to consumers.

questions.prompt: A legume field gains biologically available nitrogen after root-nodule bacteria become active. Which process most directly explains the change?
choices: Denitrification converts nitrate in the soil to N₂ gas, which roots take up
Assimilation releases nitrogen from dead tissue into the soil as nitrate
Nitrogen fixation converts atmospheric N₂ to ammonia, which becomes ammonium
Nitrification converts atmospheric N₂ directly into plant protein
questions.explanation: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert atmospheric N₂ into ammonia; in soil, ammonia quickly becomes ammonium that plants can use. The 2026–27 clarification emphasizes this microbial step.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains why less energy is available at higher trophic levels?
choices: Decomposers recycle all of that energy back up the food chain to the top consumers
Consumers make new energy as they grow, so less of it is passed upward
Producers absorb part of their energy back from the consumers that eat them
Organisms use much of the energy they take in for metabolism and release heat
questions.explanation: Energy flows through ecosystems rather than cycling. Respiration, movement, and other metabolic processes transfer much energy to the surroundings as heat.

questions.prompt: A coastal lagoon has brackish water, high nutrient input, and strong nursery habitat use by fish. Which biome description best fits?
choices: Pelagic zone
Estuary
Aphotic zone
Coral reef
questions.explanation: An estuary is a coastal area where freshwater and seawater mix. Its nutrient inputs and sheltered habitat often support high productivity and nursery functions.

questions.prompt: A producer level stores 18,000 kJ. Using the 10% rule, about how much energy is available to secondary consumers?
choices: 18 kJ
180 kJ
questions.explanation: Apply the approximate 10% transfer twice: producers to primary consumers gives 1,800 kJ; primary to secondary consumers gives 180 kJ. The rule is an approximation, not a fixed law.

questions.prompt: In a pond food web, algae → zooplankton → small fish → bass, while algae also support insect larvae eaten by small fish. If zooplankton decline sharply, which outcome is best supported?
choices: Bass must disappear immediately because their main food chain is broken
Algae must decline because fewer zooplankton are grazing on them
Small fish may partly compensate by eating more insect larvae
Energy flow from algae to every consumer in the pond stops
questions.explanation: The second prey pathway provides small fish with an alternative food source, so the food web can buffer some effects. The direction and size of other changes depend on interaction strengths.

questions.prompt: A city replaces a forest with roads and rooftops. Which immediate change is most likely during a rainstorm?
choices: More infiltration and less runoff
Less runoff because impervious surfaces store water
No change to water movement
More surface runoff and less infiltration
questions.explanation: Impervious cover reduces infiltration, so a larger share of rainfall moves quickly as surface runoff. This can also increase flooding and pollutant transport.

questions.prompt: A freshwater lake receives phosphorus-rich runoff. A bloom follows, then dissolved oxygen falls after the bloom collapses. Which sequence best explains the change?
choices: Phosphorus stimulates producers, and all resulting oxygen is permanently stored in the lake
Phosphorus stimulates producer growth; decomposers consume oxygen while breaking down dead biomass
Phosphorus directly removes dissolved oxygen before any organisms respond
Phosphorus causes denitrification to stop, which immediately kills fish
questions.explanation: Phosphorus can limit production in freshwater systems. Added phosphorus can trigger eutrophication; microbial decomposition of the resulting biomass raises oxygen demand and lowers dissolved oxygen.

questions.prompt: The distribution of terrestrial biomes is strongly shaped by long-term patterns of temperature and precipitation.
questions.explanation: Temperature and precipitation constrain plant growth and help determine characteristic biome structure. Local soils, disturbance, and other factors also matter.

questions.prompt: The phosphorus cycle has a large, rapidly exchanging atmospheric reservoir comparable to the nitrogen cycle.
questions.explanation: The major phosphorus reservoirs are phosphorus-bearing rocks and ocean sediments. The cycle lacks a significant atmospheric component, as clarified for 2026–27.

questions.prompt: What is net primary productivity (NPP)?
questions.answer: The rate at which producers store energy or biomass after subtracting their own respiration from gross primary productivity: NPP = GPP − R.
questions.explanation: NPP represents the energy available for producer growth and, indirectly, consumers. State units as a rate per area, such as kJ/m²/year.

questions.prompt: What are the main steps of the nitrogen cycle, and what role do soil microorganisms play?
questions.answer: Nitrogen fixation, assimilation, ammonification, nitrification, and denitrification move nitrogen among reservoirs. Soil microorganisms carry out or enable several steps, including fixation of N₂ into ammonia.
questions.explanation: Plants can take up nitrogen compounds such as ammonium or nitrate; atmospheric N₂ is not directly available to most organisms.

questions.prompt: How does a food web differ from a food chain, and what do arrows represent?
questions.answer: A food chain shows one pathway of energy and matter transfer; a food web links multiple chains. Arrows point from the resource eaten toward the consumer, showing energy and matter flow.
questions.explanation: Detritivores and decomposers also connect food-web pathways by processing dead matter and returning nutrients to the environment.

questions.prompt: Why does available energy generally decrease at each higher trophic level?
questions.answer: Organisms use much of the energy they consume for respiration, movement, and other life processes, and much of it dissipates as heat. Only a fraction is stored as biomass available to the next trophic level.
questions.explanation: Energy flows through ecosystems and is not recycled; matter and nutrients can cycle.

questions.prompt: A conservation survey finds several varieties of a native wildflower that differ in inherited drought tolerance. Which level of biodiversity is directly described?
choices: Species richness
Ecosystem diversity
Trophic diversity
Genetic diversity
questions.explanation: Inherited variation among members of the same species is genetic diversity. Species richness counts species; ecosystem diversity describes the variety of habitats or ecosystems.

questions.prompt: Two meadows each contain 5 plant species and 100 plants. Meadow A has 20 of each species; Meadow B has 80 of one species and 5 of each other species. Which statement is correct?
choices: A has greater richness, B has greater evenness
Both have the same richness, and A has greater evenness
B has greater richness because one species dominates
They have identical richness and evenness
questions.explanation: Both meadows contain five species, so their richness is equal. Meadow A distributes individuals more evenly among those species.

questions.prompt: A proposed reserve plan compares two habitat patches: Patch X is large and near a source forest; Patch Y is small and isolated. Island biogeography predicts that, all else equal, X will tend to support:
choices: Fewer species because large patches prevent immigration from the nearby forest
The same species count because patch area never matters
More species because immigration is easier and extinction risk is lower
Fewer species because nearby sources increase competition only
questions.explanation: Island biogeography predicts higher immigration to less isolated patches and lower extinction in larger patches, tending to produce greater species richness.

questions.prompt: Which is a regulating ecosystem service provided by a wetland?
choices: Harvesting wild rice and fish to sell at local markets
Recreation, birdwatching and outdoor education for visitors
Floodwater storage that reduces downstream flood peaks
Spiritual and aesthetic inspiration for visitors
questions.explanation: Flood regulation is a regulating service. Food is a provisioning service; recreation and aesthetic benefits are cultural services.

questions.prompt: A stream insect survives at dissolved oxygen levels of 4–12 mg/L, grows best at 8 mg/L, and disappears below 4 mg/L. A new discharge lowers oxygen from 8 to 5 mg/L. What is the strongest inference?
choices: The population is already outside its tolerance range and will soon disappear
The population must increase because lower oxygen reduces its predators
The species has genetically adapted to low oxygen within one generation
The population remains within its tolerance range but below its optimum
questions.explanation: Five mg/L is within the stated 4–12 mg/L range, but below the optimum of 8 mg/L. Performance may decline without the population being outside its tolerance.

questions.prompt: After a low-intensity fire, a grassland regains plant cover in two growing seasons, but a nearby burned forest takes decades to recover. Which property does the grassland show?
choices: Greater resilience under the disturbance described
Lower resilience to the disturbance described
Primary succession after the disturbance
Higher species richness than the forest by definition
questions.explanation: Resilience is the capacity or rate of recovery after disturbance. The grassland returned to its prior cover more quickly in this scenario.

questions.prompt: A glacier retreats, exposing bare rock with no soil. Which process is most likely to begin community development?
choices: Secondary succession begins because soil is already present
Primary succession begins on a surface lacking soil
A climax community forms before pioneer species arrive
The site undergoes no succession until all rock is weathered
questions.explanation: Primary succession begins on surfaces lacking soil. Pioneer species such as lichens and mosses can contribute to soil formation, allowing later communities to establish.

questions.prompt: A field report states: “Since highway construction divided one forest into small isolated patches, monitoring found fewer animal crossings and smaller local groups.” Which process most directly could raise extinction risk?
choices: Increased gene flow between the newly separated forest fragments
Increased interior habitat in each small fragment
Reduced habitat area and reduced movement among populations
Elimination of all edge effects along the highway corridor
questions.explanation: The report suggests reduced connectivity and smaller habitat patches. Both can limit gene flow and recolonization while making small populations more vulnerable.

questions.prompt: A warming stream favors insects that mature earlier. Which evidence would best support the claim that the population adapted through natural selection?
choices: Every individual changed its genes during its lifetime
The stream warmed, so all insects immediately became earlier-maturing
The number of insect species increased after one season
Earlier maturation is heritable and became more common across generations
questions.explanation: Natural selection acts on heritable variation. Evidence of a heritable trait increasing in frequency across generations supports evolutionary adaptation, consistent with the clarified learning objective.

questions.prompt: Species richness is the number of species present, while evenness describes how individuals are distributed among those species.
questions.explanation: Richness and evenness are distinct components of community diversity. A community can have high richness but low evenness if one species dominates.

questions.prompt: Secondary succession typically begins where soil remains after a disturbance, such as on an abandoned field.
questions.explanation: Because soil and often seeds, roots, or microbes remain, secondary succession generally proceeds faster than primary succession on bare rock.

questions.prompt: Name three levels of biodiversity and define each.
questions.answer: Genetic diversity is variation within and among populations of a species; species diversity concerns the variety and relative abundance of species; ecosystem diversity is the variety of ecosystems or habitats.
questions.explanation: These levels are related but not interchangeable. Protecting one does not automatically preserve all three.

questions.prompt: What are the four broad categories of ecosystem services?
questions.answer: Provisioning (goods such as food and timber), regulating (processes such as flood control), cultural (recreation or spiritual value), and supporting services (processes such as nutrient cycling and soil formation).
questions.explanation: Supporting services underpin many of the other benefits people receive from ecosystems.

questions.prompt: How do island area and isolation affect predicted species richness?
questions.answer: Larger islands or habitat patches tend to have lower extinction rates; less isolated ones tend to have higher immigration rates. Both factors generally raise equilibrium species richness.
questions.explanation: The model predicts patterns; habitat quality, history, species traits, and human impacts also influence actual richness.

questions.prompt: Distinguish resistance from resilience in an ecosystem.
questions.answer: Resistance is how little an ecosystem changes during a disturbance; resilience is how well or quickly it recovers afterward.
questions.explanation: An ecosystem may be resistant but recover slowly from a rare severe event, or change substantially and then recover quickly.

questions.prompt: A raccoon eats many foods and lives in cities, forests, and wetlands. Which label best describes this species?
choices: Generalist
Specialist
Indicator species
Keystone species
questions.explanation: A generalist uses a broad range of resources and habitats. Raccoons can exploit varied foods and environments.

questions.prompt: A graph description shows most individuals of a species surviving to old age, followed by a steep decline late in life. Which survivorship curve is most consistent?
choices: Type II
Type I
Type III
J-shaped population-growth curve
questions.explanation: Type I survivorship has high survival through early and middle life with mortality rising at older ages; it is common in many large mammals.

questions.prompt: A deer population in a fenced reserve rises from 80 to 240, then fluctuates between 190 and 220 as forage becomes scarce. What is the best estimate of carrying capacity?
choices: About 200 deer
About 80 deer
About 240 deer
It cannot be estimated from resource limits
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity is the population size an environment can support over time. The later fluctuations near 200 as forage becomes scarce suggest K is roughly 200.

questions.prompt: A town’s population grows from 820,000 to 902,000 in one year. What is the percent increase?
questions.explanation: Percent change = (new − original) / original × 100 = (902,000 − 820,000) / 820,000 × 100 = 10.0%.

questions.prompt: Which description best identifies logistic population growth?
choices: Growth accelerates without limit as population size rises
Population size declines at a constant rate
Births and deaths are absent
Growth slows as the population approaches carrying capacity
questions.explanation: In logistic growth, resource limits cause the per-capita growth rate to decline as population size approaches carrying capacity.

questions.prompt: A country has a crude birth rate of 28 births per 1,000 people and a crude death rate of 10 deaths per 1,000. What is its approximate rate of natural increase?
questions.explanation: RNI = CBR − CDR = 28 − 10 = 18 per 1,000. Convert to percent: 18/1,000 × 100 = 1.8%. Migration is not included in RNI.

questions.prompt: A population grows at 2% per year. Using the Rule of 70, what is its approximate doubling time?
choices: 14 years
35 years
70 years
140 years
questions.explanation: Doubling time ≈ 70 / annual growth rate in percent = 70 / 2 = 35 years. This is an estimate that assumes a roughly stable growth rate.

questions.prompt: A country’s age-structure diagram has a broad base and narrows quickly at older ages. If birth and death rates remain similar, what is most likely?
choices: The population will shrink right away because death rates stay high across every age group
Most people are already past reproductive age, so population growth will stop within a few years
A large cohort of young people will enter reproductive ages, supporting future growth
The narrow top shows strong net emigration of working-age adults
questions.explanation: A broad base indicates many young people relative to older groups. As they age into reproductive years, population momentum can sustain growth even if fertility begins to fall.

questions.prompt: A demographic summary states: “Death rates have fallen after sanitation improved, while birth rates remain high.” Which demographic-transition stage is most consistent?
choices: Stage 1, with high birth and death rates and slow growth
Stage 2, with declining death rates and rapid growth
Stage 4, with low birth and death rates and slow growth
Stage 5, with birth rates that fall below death rates
questions.explanation: The summary describes falling death rates with birth rates still high, characteristic of Stage 2 and rapid population growth.

questions.prompt: In one year a region records 12,000 births, 8,000 deaths, 3,000 immigrants, and 5,000 emigrants. What is the net population change?
choices: −2,000 people
+4,000 people
+8,000 people
+2,000 people
questions.explanation: Net change = births − deaths + immigration − emigration = 12,000 − 8,000 + 3,000 − 5,000 = +2,000 people.

questions.prompt: Researchers test whether food supply affects reproduction in a small mammal. They randomly assign equal-age females to high- and low-food enclosures, keep temperature and enclosure size constant, and count surviving offspring. Which is the dependent variable?
choices: Number of surviving offspring
Food level assigned to each enclosure
Temperature held in each enclosure
Age of the females at the start
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is the measured outcome: surviving offspring. Food level is the independent variable; temperature and enclosure size are controlled variables. Random assignment helps reduce confounding.

questions.prompt: Region A has 10 million residents using 5 resource units per person annually. Region B has 2 million residents using 20 units per person. Which has the larger annual resource demand by this simplified measure?
choices: Region B, 40 million units
They are equal at 10 million units
Region A, 50 million units
Cannot compare without population density
questions.explanation: Total demand = population × per-capita use. A: 10 million × 5 = 50 million units; B: 2 million × 20 = 40 million units. Population size and consumption per person both matter.

questions.prompt: Which factor can lower total fertility rates by increasing people’s ability to plan family size?
choices: Higher infant mortality rates alone
Reduced access to healthcare services
A higher crude death rate among adults
Access to education and family planning
questions.explanation: Education and family-planning access are associated with lower fertility in many contexts by expanding choices, delaying childbearing, and improving access to contraception.

questions.prompt: A severe late frost kills seedlings across a forest regardless of how crowded each plot is. The frost is best classified as:
choices: A density-independent factor such as a severe frost
A density-dependent factor such as competition
A density-dependent factor such as disease spread in crowded plots
A density-dependent factor such as territorial behavior
questions.explanation: A density-independent factor affects populations regardless of their density. A frost can affect sparse and dense populations alike.

questions.prompt: An oyster releases millions of larvae; few survive the first days, but survivors may live for years. Which curve and strategy best match this pattern?
choices: Type III; many offspring with high early mortality
Type I; few offspring and high parental care
Type II; constant mortality and moderate parental investment
Type I; high juvenile survival followed by mortality late in life
questions.explanation: Type III survivorship has very high mortality early in life, often paired with many offspring and little parental care. Many marine invertebrates show this pattern.

questions.prompt: A specialist species generally has a narrow niche and may be more vulnerable when its particular habitat or food source changes.
questions.explanation: Specialists use a narrow range of resources or conditions, so environmental change can affect them strongly. Vulnerability depends on the change and species traits.

questions.prompt: In an exponential-growth model, the population growth rate is fastest when the population is smallest.
questions.explanation: With a constant per-capita growth rate, absolute growth accelerates as population size increases. Real populations encounter limits, so exponential growth cannot continue indefinitely.

questions.prompt: Rate of natural increase includes immigration and emigration.
questions.explanation: RNI uses births and deaths, commonly CBR minus CDR. Total population change also depends on immigration and emigration.

questions.prompt: Carrying capacity is fixed permanently for a species in a particular location.
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity can change when food, water, habitat, climate, disease, or human management changes. It is an estimate under specified conditions.

questions.prompt: How do r-selected and K-selected species generally differ in reproductive strategy?
questions.answer: r-selected species tend to produce many small offspring, mature quickly, and provide less parental care; K-selected species tend to produce fewer, larger offspring, mature later, and provide more parental care.
questions.explanation: These are broad tendencies along a continuum, not rigid categories; actual strategies depend on environmental conditions.

questions.prompt: Give the percent-change formula for a population and define each term.
questions.answer: Percent change = (new population − initial population) / initial population × 100%. The result is positive for growth and negative for decline.
questions.explanation: Keep the initial population in the denominator and include the percent unit in the answer.

questions.prompt: What do Type I, Type II, and Type III survivorship curves show?
questions.answer: Type I: high survival until old age; Type II: roughly constant mortality risk across life; Type III: very high early mortality with greater survival among those reaching adulthood.
questions.explanation: These curves describe patterns across a population; they do not mean every individual follows the same lifespan.

questions.prompt: Summarize the demographic transition from early to later stages.
questions.answer: As sanitation, food, and health care improve, death rates often decline before birth rates, creating rapid growth; later, birth rates decline and growth slows. Some models include stable or declining population stages.
questions.explanation: The model describes a broad historical pattern; countries may differ in timing and path.

questions.prompt: What can an age-structure diagram suggest about a population’s future growth?
questions.answer: A broad base often signals many young people and potential population momentum; a more rectangular shape suggests slower growth; a narrow base with larger older cohorts can signal decline.
questions.explanation: Use the diagram with fertility, mortality, and migration data; it is not a precise forecast by itself.

questions.prompt: How do births, deaths, immigration, and emigration determine total population change?
questions.answer: Population change = births − deaths + immigration − emigration. RNI considers births minus deaths, often using crude rates; it excludes migration.
questions.explanation: For growth rate as a percentage, rate units and population size must be handled consistently. Doubling time can be estimated as 70 divided by annual percent growth.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly combines atmospheric composition and the layer containing most weather?
choices: The stratosphere contains most weather, and dry air is mostly carbon dioxide, followed by argon and then oxygen
The mesosphere contains most water vapor, while dry air is mostly hydrogen followed by helium
The thermosphere contains most weather, while dry air is mostly ozone followed by nitrogen
The troposphere contains most weather and water vapor, while dry air is mostly nitrogen followed by oxygen
questions.explanation: Most weather and atmospheric water vapor are in the troposphere. Dry air near Earth’s surface is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, with smaller amounts of other gases.

questions.prompt: At which plate boundary is new oceanic crust most commonly formed?
choices: Convergent boundary where one plate subducts
Divergent boundary where plates move apart
Transform boundary where plates slide past
Continental collision zone only
questions.explanation: At divergent boundaries, rising magma cools as plates separate and creates new crust, such as along mid-ocean ridges.

questions.prompt: A mineral soil sample is 40% sand, 40% silt, and 20% clay. Using the soil texture triangle, which class best fits?
choices: Clay
Sandy loam
Loam
Silt
questions.explanation: The percentages sum to 100%, and the 40% sand, 40% silt, 20% clay combination falls in the loam class on a standard soil texture triangle. Loam balances particle sizes and often supports crops.

questions.prompt: A parcel of air moving northward in the Northern Hemisphere is deflected to the right relative to its direction of travel. Which effect explains this?
choices: A pressure gradient force
The greenhouse effect
The Coriolis effect from Earth’s rotation
Convection caused by local surface heating
questions.explanation: Earth’s rotation produces the Coriolis effect: moving air and water are deflected right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.prompt: Moist air rises over a mountain, cools, and releases precipitation on the western slope. The eastern slope is much drier. What best explains the dry eastern slope?
choices: A cold ocean current that removes precipitation on the leeward slope
A sea breeze carrying moist air away from the mountain
A temperature inversion that forces all water vapor downward
A rain shadow as descending air warms and dries
questions.explanation: Air loses moisture as it rises and cools on the windward slope. Descending air on the leeward side warms and has lower relative humidity, creating a rain shadow.

questions.prompt: After a pesticide is applied on a hillside, which area is most directly connected to the receiving stream by surface runoff?
choices: The watershed draining to that stream
The neighboring watershed separated by a topographic divide
Only the narrow riparian strip along the stream
Every watershed in the same state
questions.explanation: A watershed is the land area that drains surface water to a common outlet. Runoff can carry pesticides from locations within that drainage area to the stream.

questions.prompt: A farm leaves bare soil on a steep slope through the rainy season. Which change would most directly reduce soil erosion?
choices: Increasing the length of the bare slope
Planting cover crops and contouring rows
Removing the remaining vegetation at field edges
Tilling rows up and down the slope
questions.explanation: Cover crops protect soil from raindrop impact and bind it with roots; contour farming slows downslope water flow. Both can reduce erosion.

questions.prompt: Why does a location near the equator generally receive more direct solar energy per unit area than a high-latitude location?
choices: Earth's orbit brings the equator closer to the Sun than it brings the poles
The equator has more hours of daylight than the poles on every day of the year
Sunlight arrives at a higher angle and is concentrated over a smaller surface area
Thinner air over the equator lets far more of the incoming sunlight reach the ground
questions.explanation: More direct rays concentrate incoming solar energy over a smaller surface area. At high latitudes, sunlight arrives at a lower angle and is spread over a larger area.

questions.prompt: A fisheries bulletin states: “During El Niño, weakened trade winds allow warm surface water to spread eastward across the tropical Pacific.” Which local change is likely off western South America?
choices: Stronger cold-water upwelling and greater nutrient supply to the coast
No change, because surface winds do not affect ocean currents or upwelling
Permanent cooling of the entire Pacific
Reduced upwelling and often lower nutrient supply to surface waters
questions.explanation: The bulletin describes weakened trade winds and eastward warm-water movement. El Niño weakens normal upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water off South America, often reducing nutrient availability. Impacts vary by event.

questions.prompt: A coastal current brings cold, nutrient-rich deep water to the surface. Which process is being described?
choices: Upwelling
Downwelling
Thermal inversion
Subduction of continental crust
questions.explanation: Upwelling moves deeper water toward the surface, supplying nutrients that can support high primary productivity and fisheries.

questions.prompt: A soil profile has a dark, organic-rich surface layer above a zone where clay and iron accumulate. Which horizons are most likely described?
choices: O above A
A above B
B above C
C above R
questions.explanation: The A horizon is mineral topsoil enriched with organic matter; materials leached from upper horizons can accumulate in the B horizon below. An O horizon is mostly surface litter and organic material.

questions.prompt: Two equal-size watersheds receive the same 25 mm storm. Forest basin runoff is 6 mm; urban basin runoff is 18 mm. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Forest runoff was three times urban runoff, suggesting that forest soils absorbed less of the storm
Runoff was equal in both basins because the rainfall depth was the same
Urban runoff was three times forest runoff, consistent with less infiltration from impervious cover
The data establish that the urban basin had no infiltration at all during the storm
questions.explanation: 18 mm / 6 mm = 3, so recorded runoff depth in the urban basin was three times as large. Impervious surfaces can reduce infiltration; equal storm depth helps comparison but does not control all watershed differences.

questions.prompt: A temperature profile shows air temperature decreasing with altitude from the surface to 10 km, then increasing from 10 to 50 km. Which layer and process best explain the reversal?
choices: Mesopause; sunlight reflected off the surface and clouds warms the mesosphere aloft
Stratopause; latent heat released by clouds warms the upper troposphere and above
Thermopause; heat carried upward from warm ocean currents warms the stratosphere above
Tropopause; ozone absorption of ultraviolet radiation warms the stratosphere aloft
questions.explanation: The troposphere generally cools with altitude; above the tropopause, stratospheric ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation, producing a temperature increase with altitude through much of the stratosphere.

questions.prompt: Water slowly dissolves limestone and enlarges cracks into caves. Which process is occurring?
choices: Chemical weathering
Mechanical weathering only
Deposition
Plate divergence
questions.explanation: Chemical weathering changes minerals through reactions such as dissolution. Mechanical weathering breaks material into smaller pieces without changing its chemical composition.

questions.prompt: Which process returns liquid water from plant leaves to the atmosphere?
choices: Infiltration
Transpiration
Percolation
Condensation
questions.explanation: Transpiration is water vapor released from plants, mainly through leaf stomata. It contributes to evapotranspiration along with evaporation from surfaces.

questions.prompt: Soil forms through interactions among weathered parent material, organic matter, climate, organisms, topography, and time.
questions.explanation: These soil-forming factors influence soil development, horizons, and properties over time.

questions.prompt: The Coriolis effect deflects moving air to the left in the Northern Hemisphere and to the right in the Southern Hemisphere.
questions.explanation: The deflection is to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.prompt: Climate describes long-term patterns of atmospheric conditions, whereas weather describes short-term conditions.
questions.explanation: Climate summarizes long-term averages and variability; weather refers to atmospheric conditions over shorter time scales.

questions.prompt: La Niña is generally associated with stronger-than-usual trade winds and enhanced upwelling in parts of the eastern tropical Pacific.
questions.explanation: La Niña tends to strengthen the normal Pacific pattern, including trade winds and eastern-Pacific upwelling, though regional effects vary.

questions.prompt: What are common soil horizons in a developed soil profile?
questions.answer: O: surface organic litter; A: topsoil with minerals and organic matter; E: eluviation or leaching layer where present; B: subsoil where materials accumulate; C: partially weathered parent material; R: bedrock.
questions.explanation: Not every profile has every horizon, and horizon thickness and properties vary by location.

questions.prompt: How does unequal solar heating help drive global circulation?
questions.answer: Unequal heating creates temperature and pressure differences. Air rises in warmer regions, sinks in cooler regions, and moves between pressure zones; Earth’s rotation deflects these flows.
questions.explanation: The simplified global pattern is modified by seasons, continents, topography, and ocean-atmosphere interactions.

questions.prompt: Define a watershed and explain one way it links land use to water quality.
questions.answer: A watershed is the land area that drains to a shared outlet. Rain can carry sediments, nutrients, pesticides, and other pollutants from land uses in that area into connected streams or lakes.
questions.explanation: Watershed boundaries follow topography, and groundwater connections may also matter.

questions.prompt: Describe how a mountain can create a rain-shadow climate.
questions.answer: Moist air rises on the windward side, cools, and loses moisture as precipitation. Air descending on the leeward side warms and becomes relatively dry, producing less precipitation.
questions.explanation: The strength of the effect depends on wind direction, mountain height, and regional climate.

questions.prompt: Compare typical tropical Pacific conditions during El Niño and La Niña.
questions.answer: El Niño features weakened trade winds and unusually warm central/eastern tropical Pacific surface waters, often reducing eastern-Pacific upwelling. La Niña generally strengthens trade winds and cools those waters, often enhancing upwelling.
questions.explanation: Both shift rainfall and climate patterns around the world, but effects vary by region and event.

questions.prompt: How does the soil texture triangle classify soil, and why can loam support many crops?
questions.answer: The triangle uses percentages of sand, silt, and clay, which sum to 100%, to assign a texture class. Loam blends these particle sizes, often balancing drainage, aeration, and water and nutrient retention.
questions.explanation: Texture is only one part of soil quality; organic matter, structure, pH, and climate also affect crop suitability.

questions.prompt: Several fishing boats harvest from an open-access bay. Each boat benefits from catching more fish, while the cost of stock decline is shared. Which concept does this illustrate?
choices: Tragedy of the commons
Maximum sustainable yield
Privatization of a resource
A negative externality from an identifiable point source
questions.explanation: When individuals gain from using a shared resource but share the depletion costs, private incentives can lead to overuse. Access rules or collective management can reduce this pressure.

questions.prompt: A farmer cooperative report says: “High-yield seed and irrigation raised harvests, but fertilizer and pesticide use also increased.” Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The report establishes that fertilizer alone caused the entire harvest increase across the region
Input-intensive methods can raise yields while creating runoff and chemical-exposure trade-offs
The report shows that every farm will have the same yield response to new seed and irrigation
The increased harvest proves that pesticide use has no environmental cost
questions.explanation: The report supports a yield gain alongside increased input use, which can raise environmental risks. It does not establish the magnitude of the effect at every farm or prove a universal outcome.

questions.prompt: Which irrigation method generally delivers water directly near plant roots and can reduce evaporation compared with broad surface flooding?
choices: Flood irrigation
Unlined canal seepage
Drip irrigation
Overhead spraying at midday
questions.explanation: Drip systems deliver water near roots, often reducing evaporation and runoff. Costs, maintenance, clogging, and energy needs can limit adoption.

questions.prompt: A farm plants one crop species across thousands of hectares. What is a common ecological risk of this monoculture?
choices: The field necessarily contains more crop species as the planted area keeps growing
Uniform planting prevents pests from moving between plants of the same species
The crop becomes resistant to every disease without any selection taking place
A specialist pest may spread readily through a large area of similar host plants
questions.explanation: Monocultures reduce crop diversity, so a pest or disease specialized on that crop can spread widely. Uniform fields may also need more management inputs.

questions.prompt: A farm applies 1,000 m³ of irrigation water, and 650 m³ reaches crop roots for plant use. What is the application efficiency?
questions.explanation: Efficiency = useful water / applied water × 100 = 650 m³ / 1,000 m³ × 100 = 65%. The remaining 35% is lost or unavailable to roots through runoff, evaporation, or seepage.

questions.prompt: A dry-region field is irrigated repeatedly with salty groundwater, and evaporation is high. Why can soil salinity rise?
choices: Plants convert the dissolved salts into nitrogen fertilizer that builds up in the soil
Salts evaporate faster than water and settle back onto the soil surface
Water evaporates while dissolved salts remain and accumulate in the root zone
Irrigation always flushes salts away, even where there is no drainage
questions.explanation: Evaporation removes water but leaves dissolved salts behind. Without sufficient drainage and leaching, salts can accumulate and make it harder for plants to take up water.

questions.prompt: A grower monitors pest abundance, sets an action threshold, encourages beneficial insects, and sprays only if needed. Which approach is being used?
choices: Calendar-based spraying
Single-method biocontrol
Rotation without monitoring
Integrated pest management
questions.explanation: IPM combines monitoring, biological and cultural controls, and targeted chemical control when pest levels justify it. It aims to reduce unnecessary pesticide use, not guarantee zero pesticide use.

questions.prompt: After heavy rain, a stream below fertilized fields shows higher nitrate levels. Which source is most likely?
choices: Nonpoint runoff carrying fertilizer from many field areas
A single pipe discharge from a wastewater plant
Natural weathering of bedrock within the stream channel
Atmospheric nitrogen fixation occurring in the stream
questions.explanation: Fertilizer can be transported by runoff from diffuse areas, making it nonpoint-source pollution. Vegetated buffer strips and careful nutrient timing can reduce transport.

questions.prompt: A grazing report states: “Pasture sections were rested between grazing periods, and vegetation cover improved; runoff still increased near a stream crossing.” Which interpretation is strongest?
choices: Rotational grazing improved cover in this case, but livestock access can still create localized runoff
The report proves that rotational grazing removes every environmental impact on the land and stream
More vegetation cover proves that no runoff occurred anywhere on the rested pasture sections at all
A stream crossing has no relation to erosion, so the extra runoff must come from heavier rainfall alone
questions.explanation: The report supports improved cover alongside a remaining runoff issue near the crossing. Management benefits can be real without eliminating all impacts.

questions.prompt: Which practice is most likely to retain more habitat structure than clear-cutting an entire forest stand?
choices: Clear-cutting the entire stand in one operation
Selective harvesting of chosen trees while retaining much of the stand canopy
Removing all mature trees in stages through a shelterwood harvest
Harvesting every tree in a series of small patches until the whole stand is cut
questions.explanation: Selective harvest can preserve more canopy and habitat structure than clear-cutting, though outcomes depend on intensity, roads, and regeneration practices. It may cost more and reduce short-term timber yield.

questions.prompt: A mine is proposed near a stream. Which management choice most directly reduces the risk of acid mine drainage?
choices: Allow tailings to contact air and runoff, then begin monitoring only after fish decline
Dilute acidic drainage downstream without controlling its source
Store sulfide-bearing waste in covered, lined areas and collect drainage for treatment
Remove riparian vegetation to speed water flow past the mine
questions.explanation: Oxidation of sulfide minerals can generate acidic drainage that mobilizes metals. Encapsulation, water management, and treatment reduce risk, but monitoring and long-term maintenance may be needed.

questions.prompt: A fishery reports declining catch per unit effort and many juvenile fish in the catch. Which management response best addresses the likely problem?
choices: Increase harvest quotas based on a single year of unusually high catch data
Open additional fishing grounds while keeping total fishing effort unchanged
Switch to gear that targets juvenile fish while leaving the total catch unlimited
Set evidence-based catch limits and protect nursery habitat or juvenile fish
questions.explanation: Declining catch per unit effort can indicate reduced stock abundance, and juvenile harvest reduces future recruitment. Catch limits, gear rules, seasonal closures, and habitat protection can help rebuild stocks.

questions.prompt: A coastal community considers intensive shrimp aquaculture in a mangrove area. Which assessment best captures a potential trade-off?
choices: It may increase seafood production and jobs, but clearing mangroves can remove nursery habitat and coastal protection
It can avoid some wild-stock pressure if feed, effluent, and siting are managed, so those factors should be assessed
It improves biodiversity wherever ponds replace mangroves
Its only environmental concern is the visual appearance of ponds
questions.explanation: Aquaculture can produce seafood and jobs, but siting, feed, waste, disease, and habitat conversion matter. Avoiding mangrove conversion and managing effluent can reduce, not eliminate, impacts.

questions.prompt: A city of 2 million people has an average ecological footprint of 4 global hectares per person. A proposed plan lowers the average to 3.5. What is the projected reduction in total footprint?
choices: 0.5 million global hectares
1 million global hectares
7 million global hectares
8 million global hectares
questions.explanation: Initial total = 2 million × 4 = 8 million global hectares. Projected total = 2 million × 3.5 = 7 million; reduction = 1 million global hectares. This assumes population is unchanged.

questions.prompt: A city compares concrete drains with permeable pavement, trees, and restored wetlands. Which evaluation is strongest?
choices: Concrete drains move water away quickly, so they remove all downstream flood risk for the city and its neighbors
Permeable pavement works equally well on every soil type and at any water table depth, so no site testing is needed
Green infrastructure can capture and infiltrate runoff and add habitat, but needs suitable sites and maintenance
Wetlands need no land, upkeep, or storm-capacity planning once they have been restored
questions.explanation: Green infrastructure can increase infiltration and storage while providing co-benefits, but it has space and maintenance costs and cannot guarantee protection during every extreme event.

questions.prompt: Crop rotation can interrupt some pest cycles and help maintain soil fertility when crops have different nutrient needs.
questions.explanation: Rotating crops can disrupt specialized pests and, when legumes are included, add biologically fixed nitrogen. Benefits depend on crop choices and local conditions.

questions.prompt: Synthetic nitrogen fertilizer can increase crop production, but excess application can contribute to nitrate runoff or leaching.
questions.explanation: Applying fertilizer at rates and times matched to crop uptake can lower losses while maintaining yields.

questions.prompt: All pasture-based livestock systems use less land per unit of protein than all feedlot systems.
questions.explanation: Land use varies by species, stocking rate, feed, and production system. Pasture systems generally require more land, while environmental effects differ by practice and site.

questions.prompt: Clear-cutting can increase erosion and habitat loss, although its impacts depend on site conditions and whether protective measures and regeneration are used.
questions.explanation: Removing tree cover can expose soil and simplify habitat. Buffers, slope limits, and replanting can reduce some impacts but do not make every harvest impact-free.

questions.prompt: What was the Green Revolution, and what practices helped raise crop yields?
questions.answer: The Green Revolution was a period of major increases in crop yields associated with high-yield crop varieties, expanded irrigation, synthetic fertilizers, pesticides, and mechanization.
questions.explanation: Yield gains varied by region and crop, and input-intensive methods can have trade-offs such as water demand, runoff, and pesticide impacts.

questions.prompt: What are the core steps or principles of integrated pest management (IPM)?
questions.answer: Monitor pests and beneficial organisms, identify the pest, set an action threshold, prioritize prevention and biological or cultural controls, and use targeted pesticides when needed.
questions.explanation: IPM manages pests while minimizing risk and unnecessary chemical use; it does not require never using pesticides.

questions.prompt: On a global scale, about how much human freshwater consumption goes to agriculture, and how do irrigation methods differ?
questions.answer: Approximately 70% is used for agriculture. Drip delivers water near roots and can reduce evaporation but costs more and may clog; spray loses water to evaporation and wind; flood is simple but may be inefficient and can cause waterlogging or salinization.
questions.explanation: The approximately 70% figure is the 2026–27 College Board clarification. Irrigation efficiency varies with system design, climate, crop, soil, maintenance, and water pricing.

questions.prompt: Compare environmental trade-offs of CAFOs and pasture-based or rotational grazing systems.
questions.answer: CAFOs can use land and feed efficiently per unit of product and lower consumer costs, but concentrated manure, nutrient pollution, and antibiotic-resistance risks require management. Pasture systems can return manure to soils and rotational grazing may reduce overgrazing, but they use more land and can still cause runoff and erosion.
questions.explanation: Impacts vary with livestock type and practice; not all pasture systems are antibiotic-free.

questions.prompt: Give two ways to manage a fishery sustainably and explain how each helps.
questions.answer: Set catch limits using stock assessments and enforce them; protect spawning seasons or nursery habitat; use selective gear to reduce bycatch; or establish well-designed no-take areas.
questions.explanation: Management must consider monitoring, compliance, community livelihoods, and how fish move beyond protected boundaries.

questions.prompt: How can soil conservation and nutrient management reduce agricultural impacts while maintaining production?
questions.answer: Use practices such as cover crops, contour farming, reduced tillage, riparian buffers, crop rotation, and nutrient application matched to crop demand. These can limit erosion and nutrient loss while protecting soil, but require site-specific planning and may have cost or labor trade-offs.
questions.explanation: No single practice works everywhere; evaluate yield, water, soil, biodiversity, and farm economics together.

questions.prompt: Which energy resource is nonrenewable on human time scales?
choices: Wind
Sunlight
Geothermal heat
Coal
questions.explanation: Coal forms over geologic time and is depleted as it is extracted, so it is nonrenewable on human time scales.

questions.prompt: Which option is a renewable energy source when managed so use does not exceed regeneration?
choices: Uranium ore from open-pit mines
Coal from deep seams
Biomass from regrowing forests
Oil pumped from deep offshore wells
questions.explanation: Biomass can be renewable if vegetation regrows at a rate that sustains harvest. Unsustainable harvest can still deplete forests and release net emissions.

questions.prompt: How much energy is equivalent to 1 kilowatt-hour (kWh)?
choices: 3.6 megajoules (MJ)
36 megajoules (MJ)
0.36 megajoules (MJ)
1,000 megajoules (MJ)
questions.explanation: 1 kWh = 1,000 watts × 3,600 seconds = 3,600,000 joules = 3.6 MJ.

questions.prompt: Which fossil fuel generally produces the greatest carbon dioxide emissions per unit of energy when burned?
choices: Natural gas
Coal
Hydrogen
Wind
questions.explanation: Coal generally releases more CO₂ per unit of energy than oil or natural gas when combusted. Mining and combustion also cause other environmental impacts.

questions.prompt: A generator converts 200 MJ of fuel energy into 70 MJ of electricity. What is its conversion efficiency?
questions.explanation: Efficiency = useful output / input × 100 = 70 MJ / 200 MJ × 100 = 35%. The remaining input energy is mostly lost as heat.

questions.prompt: A household uses 500 kWh of electricity. Using 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ, how much energy is this?
choices: 180 MJ
questions.explanation: 500 kWh × 3.6 MJ/kWh = 1,800 MJ. The kWh units cancel, leaving megajoules.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the environmental impacts of hydraulic fracturing is accurate?
choices: Its only documented impact is temporary noise and truck traffic near the well pad
It cannot affect groundwater at all, because every well is lined with steel and cement
Induced earthquakes from wastewater disposal occur only in volcanic regions
Groundwater contamination, methane leakage and induced seismicity are all possible impacts
questions.explanation: Potential impacts include groundwater contamination, volatile organic compound releases, methane leakage, and induced seismicity associated with some wastewater disposal. Risks depend on practices and site conditions.

questions.prompt: Which statement accurately describes nuclear fission power generation?
choices: Fission releases heat that can make steam to turn a turbine, while producing radioactive waste that requires management
Fission burns uranium like a chemical fuel and releases carbon dioxide, but it produces no long-lived radioactive waste
Fission converts matter directly into electricity, so the plant needs no turbines, no steam and no cooling water at all
Fission splits water molecules to release hydrogen, which is then burned to spin a generator
questions.explanation: Fission releases heat, which is commonly used to make steam that drives a turbine-generator. Operation has low direct greenhouse-gas emissions, but radioactive waste and accident risks require management.

questions.prompt: A building uses south-facing windows and thermal mass to capture and store sunlight without photovoltaic panels. This is primarily:
choices: Active solar heating
Photovoltaic generation
Passive solar design
Solar water heating
questions.explanation: Passive solar design uses building orientation, windows, shading, and thermal mass to manage sunlight without PV panels.

questions.prompt: A wind farm’s output falls when wind speeds are very low. Which grid strategy can help manage this variability?
choices: Build more wind turbines without adding any flexibility, storage or new transmission lines
Rely on a single storage technology sized for every possible weather event
Curtail all other generation sources whenever wind output changes at all
Combine wind with storage, transmission, demand response, and other generation sources
questions.explanation: Wind output varies with weather and time. Storage, grid connections, flexible demand, forecasting, and a diverse mix can help balance supply; each has costs and constraints.

questions.prompt: A proposed dam would provide dispatchable electricity but flood a forest valley and block fish migration. Which evaluation is most complete?
choices: Count annual electricity output alone and assume reservoir, sediment and river conditions never change
Compare only fish passage costs while ignoring displaced communities and inundated habitat
Assume hydropower has no ecological effects because the water that drives it is renewable
Compare reliability and low operating emissions with habitat, sediment, flow, and community impacts
questions.explanation: Hydropower can provide controllable electricity and low operational emissions, but dams can alter habitats, sediment, water flow, fish migration, and communities. Impacts vary by design and location.

questions.prompt: A forestry brief claims: “Burning harvested wood is carbon-neutral because new trees regrow.” Which evidence is most important to evaluate?
choices: Whether regrowth timing and supply-chain emissions offset combustion and land-use emissions
Whether the harvested wood contains more carbon per tonne than the same mass of coal does
Whether the replanted tree species photosynthesize faster than the species that were cut down
Whether the wood can be transported to the power plant by rail
questions.explanation: The claim depends on the time required for regrowth, what would have happened to the land otherwise, and emissions from harvesting and processing. Carbon neutrality is not automatic.

questions.prompt: A geothermal plant is proposed where underground heat is abundant but water is scarce. Which concern should planners evaluate?
choices: Whether the plant can collect enough sunlight to keep its turbines running through the winter months
Whether the underground heat is being replenished by coal combustion at a nearby power plant
Whether the system can meet its water needs and manage subsurface fluids at this water-limited site
Whether the turbines can run for several decades without any maintenance or inspection
questions.explanation: Geothermal potential is location-specific, and some systems use substantial water or require reinjection and careful reservoir management. Designs that reduce water demand have other costs.

questions.prompt: A power plant burns 1,000 MJ of fuel at 35% efficiency. Its electricity then travels through a grid with 90% delivery efficiency. How much electrical energy reaches customers?
choices: 315 MJ
350 MJ
900 MJ
questions.explanation: First generation output = 1,000 MJ × 0.35 = 350 MJ. Delivered energy = 350 MJ × 0.90 = 315 MJ. Applying both efficiencies gives 1,000 × 0.35 × 0.90 = 315 MJ.

questions.prompt: A utility planning note says: “Wind output varies by hour; demand peaks after sunset; transmission links and storage are under review.” Which portfolio choice best responds to this evidence?
choices: Rely on wind alone and accept outages whenever output drops after sunset, since storage and new transmission are costly
Build generation only for average demand and let evening peaks go unserved until the transmission review is finished
Raise demand during windy hours so existing equipment runs more often, and postpone any decisions about storage
Combine efficiency, suitable renewables, storage or flexible demand, transmission, and firm low-carbon power
questions.explanation: The note identifies a timing mismatch and grid tools under review. A diversified portfolio can support reliability while lowering fossil-fuel use, but its mix depends on costs, resources, and local constraints.

questions.prompt: An energy source can be renewable and still create environmental impacts.
questions.explanation: Renewable sources can affect land, habitat, water, materials, and communities. Renewable describes replenishment, not absence of impact.

questions.prompt: If a device becomes more energy efficient, it always causes total energy consumption to fall.
questions.explanation: Efficiency lowers energy required per service, but total use may remain level or rise if people use the service more.

questions.prompt: Natural gas combustion releases less carbon dioxide per unit of energy than coal combustion, but methane leakage can reduce its climate advantage.
questions.explanation: Methane is a potent greenhouse gas. The climate effect of gas depends on leakage rates, infrastructure, and the time horizon used.

questions.prompt: Solar photovoltaic panels generate electricity directly from sunlight, while solar thermal systems capture sunlight as heat.
questions.explanation: PV cells convert light to electrical energy; solar thermal systems collect heat, which may be used directly or to generate electricity.

questions.prompt: Define energy efficiency and give the standard calculation.
questions.answer: Energy efficiency = useful energy output ÷ energy input × 100%. It is a percentage and is below 100% for real energy conversions.
questions.explanation: Use the same energy units for output and input so units cancel.

questions.prompt: Convert between kilowatt-hours and megajoules.
questions.answer: 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ. Multiply kWh by 3.6 to get MJ; divide MJ by 3.6 to get kWh.
questions.explanation: For example, 250 kWh × 3.6 MJ/kWh = 900 MJ.

questions.prompt: What factors help explain differences in energy consumption among countries and across time?
questions.answer: Population size, income, industrial activity, climate, access to energy, technology, energy prices, and efficiency all influence total and per-capita energy use.
questions.explanation: Total energy use and per-capita use answer different questions; a large population can have high total use even when use per person is moderate.

questions.prompt: Outline how a nuclear fission power plant generates electricity and name two management concerns.
questions.answer: Fission releases heat; the heat produces steam that turns a turbine connected to a generator. Management concerns include radioactive waste, accident risk, water use, and fuel-cycle impacts.
questions.explanation: Nuclear power has low direct operational greenhouse-gas emissions, but it is not impact-free.

questions.prompt: Give three ways a city can reduce energy consumption without reducing essential services.
questions.answer: Improve building insulation and efficient heating/cooling; expand transit, walking, and cycling; use efficient street lighting and appliances; reduce peak demand through controls and demand response.
questions.explanation: Efficiency and conservation measures may require upfront investment but can reduce energy bills and emissions over time.

questions.prompt: What factors should be compared when choosing an energy portfolio for a region?
questions.answer: Compare lifecycle emissions, reliability and dispatchability, cost, resource availability, land and water use, pollution, safety, storage and transmission needs, construction time, and community impacts.
questions.explanation: There is no universally best source mix; trade-offs and local constraints determine a defensible portfolio.

questions.prompt: Which is a primary air pollutant emitted directly from a source?
choices: Ground-level ozone formed in sunlight
Acid deposition formed from atmospheric reactions
Sulfur dioxide from a power plant stack
Photochemical smog as a mixture
questions.explanation: Sulfur dioxide can be emitted directly, so it is primary. Ground-level ozone forms in the atmosphere from precursors and is secondary.

questions.prompt: Ground-level ozone in photochemical smog forms most readily when which conditions occur together?
choices: Sulfur dioxide and particulate matter settle out during rain
Nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight
Carbon monoxide reacts with radon in cold air
Methane reacts with water vapor in darkness
questions.explanation: Sunlight drives reactions involving nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds that produce ground-level ozone and other photochemical smog components.

questions.prompt: A city wants to reduce recurrent afternoon ground-level ozone peaks. Which action most directly targets the pollutant precursors?
choices: Reduce NOx and VOC emissions from vehicles and solvent use
Reduce sulfur dioxide alone while leaving NOx and VOC emissions unchanged
Install indoor air filters in homes without changing outdoor emissions
Increase traffic flow so exhaust is diluted near roadways
questions.explanation: Ground-level ozone forms from NOx and VOC reactions in sunlight. Reducing these precursors through source controls can lower ozone formation; the mix of controls should reflect local atmospheric chemistry.

questions.prompt: A valley experiences a thermal inversion overnight: cool air is trapped beneath warmer air, and winds are weak. What is a likely consequence?
choices: Stable warm air above cooler surface air limits vertical mixing and can trap pollutants
Strong convection rapidly mixes the entire air column
An inversion removes emissions from the valley before sunrise
Warm air at the surface rises freely through cooler air above
questions.explanation: The warm layer above suppresses vertical mixing, and weak winds limit horizontal dispersion. Pollutants emitted near the surface can build up until conditions change.

questions.prompt: A monitor records PM₂.₅ concentrations of 12, 28, and 24 µg/m³ on three consecutive days. Which conclusion is supported?
choices: The three-day mean concentration was exactly 24 µg/m³
The lowest concentration of the three occurred on the second day
The concentration peaked on the second day and declined on the third
The day-to-day pattern identifies road traffic as the main source
questions.explanation: The values show an increase from 12 to 28 µg/m³ followed by a decrease to 24 µg/m³. Concentration data alone do not identify the source.

questions.prompt: A county air-quality plan explains: “The Clean Air Act authorizes EPA to set ambient standards for common pollutants; states develop plans to attain them.” Which conclusion follows?
choices: The Clean Air Act sets only indoor radon limits, which each state then enforces in homes and schools
NAAQS regulate vehicle tailpipe emissions but not ambient pollutant concentrations
The same numeric standard applies worldwide to all greenhouse gases and pollutants
The standards address outdoor air quality, with federal standards and state implementation roles
questions.explanation: The plan accurately describes a shared federal and state role: EPA sets NAAQS, and states develop implementation plans. The standards cover criteria pollutants and protect public health or welfare.

questions.prompt: A lake’s pH declines near a region that burns sulfur-rich coal. Which atmospheric pathway most directly contributes?
choices: SO₂ can form sulfuric acid compounds that return in wet or dry deposition
CO₂ dissolves in seawater and lowers ocean pH, which then spreads to inland lakes
NOx and VOCs react in sunlight to form ground-level ozone downwind of the coal plant
CFCs release chlorine that destroys stratospheric ozone above the region
questions.explanation: Sulfur dioxide can react in the atmosphere to form sulfuric acid compounds that return as acid deposition. Nitrogen oxides also contribute to acid deposition.

questions.prompt: An airtight home has elevated radon, a radioactive gas that can enter from soil through foundation gaps. Which action most directly reduces exposure?
choices: Use a HEPA filter to remove radon gas from room air
Test for radon and install a system that vents soil gas outdoors
Open a window once and assume long-term levels are controlled
Seal foundation cracks without testing or checking whether pressure changes
questions.explanation: Testing identifies elevated radon. A mitigation system commonly depressurizes soil beneath the building and vents radon outdoors; sealing alone may not solve the problem.

questions.prompt: A facility emits 800 kg of SO₂ per day. A scrubber removes 75% of the SO₂ entering it. If all emissions pass through the scrubber, how much SO₂ remains emitted per day?
choices: 200 kg/day
600 kg/day
750 kg/day
800 kg/day
questions.explanation: Removed mass = 800 kg/day × 0.75 = 600 kg/day. Remaining emissions = 800 − 600 = 200 kg/day, or 25% of the original.

questions.prompt: A thermal inversion can trap pollutants near the ground by limiting vertical air mixing.
questions.explanation: During an inversion, temperature increases with height through a layer, inhibiting the upward movement of cooler surface air and slowing pollutant dispersion.

questions.prompt: Ground-level ozone is emitted directly from vehicle tailpipes as a primary pollutant.
questions.explanation: Tailpipes emit ozone precursors such as NOx and VOCs; ground-level ozone forms secondarily through atmospheric reactions in sunlight.

questions.prompt: What is radon, and why can it be a health concern indoors?
questions.answer: Radon is a naturally occurring radioactive gas that can move from soil into buildings through openings in foundations. Long-term inhalation increases lung-cancer risk; testing and mitigation reduce exposure.
questions.explanation: Radon is odorless, so measurement is needed to identify elevated indoor concentrations.

questions.prompt: How does acid deposition form, and name one environmental effect.
questions.answer: Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides react in the atmosphere to form acidic compounds that return in precipitation or as dry deposition. It can acidify lakes and soils and damage forests or aquatic organisms.
questions.explanation: Effects depend on deposition rates and the buffering capacity of local soils and waters.

questions.prompt: Compare PM₂.₅ and ground-level ozone as air pollutants.
questions.answer: PM₂.₅ is fine particulate matter that can penetrate deep into the lungs and is emitted or formed through atmospheric reactions. Ground-level ozone is a secondary gas formed when NOx and VOCs react in sunlight.
questions.explanation: Both can harm respiratory and cardiovascular health; ozone is not emitted directly from tailpipes.

questions.prompt: What is noise pollution, and give two ways communities can reduce harmful exposure.
questions.answer: Noise pollution is unwanted or excessive sound that can disrupt sleep, communication, health, or wildlife. Communities can use quieter equipment, traffic controls, sound barriers, zoning, insulation, or green buffers.
questions.explanation: Controls should target the source and affected receptors; barriers do not eliminate every low-frequency or indoor exposure.

questions.prompt: Which is a point source of water pollution?
choices: Fertilizer washed from many fields
Sediment runoff from scattered construction sites
A wastewater pipe discharging into a river
Oil residues washed from many streets
questions.explanation: A point source is a single, identifiable discharge such as a pipe. Runoff from broad areas is generally nonpoint pollution.

questions.prompt: Which measurement directly reports the amount of oxygen dissolved in a water sample?
choices: Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD)
Turbidity only
Fecal coliform bacteria count
Dissolved oxygen concentration
questions.explanation: Dissolved oxygen (DO) is the oxygen present in water, often reported in mg/L. It supports aquatic organisms and can be affected by temperature and decomposition.

questions.prompt: Which action follows the most preferred levels of the waste hierarchy?
choices: Recycle materials after they have become waste
Incinerate waste before considering material recovery
Landfill usable items rather than preventing waste
Reduce unnecessary packaging before relying on disposal
questions.explanation: Source reduction prevents waste from being created, generally avoiding more impacts than disposal. Reuse and recycling also reduce waste but require materials and energy.

questions.prompt: Two stream samples start at 8 mg/L dissolved oxygen. After five days, Sample A has 2 mg/L and Sample B has 6 mg/L. Which sample had the greater approximate BOD over the test period?
choices: Sample B, about 2 mg/L oxygen consumed
Sample A, about 6 mg/L oxygen consumed
Both samples, about 6 mg/L because initial oxygen was equal
Cannot compare because starting oxygen is unknown
questions.explanation: Approximate oxygen consumed = initial DO − final DO. A: 8 − 2 = 6 mg/L; B: 8 − 6 = 2 mg/L. Greater BOD indicates more oxygen was used by microbes decomposing organic matter.

questions.prompt: A lake receives excess phosphorus fertilizer runoff. Which sequence most directly leads to a fish kill?
choices: Nutrient input → increased plant growth → permanent increase in dissolved oxygen
Nutrient input → lower algal growth → decomposition stops
Nutrient input → algal growth → decomposition → dissolved oxygen decline
Nutrient input → water clarification → immediate fish mortality
questions.explanation: Excess nutrients can stimulate algal blooms. When algae die, microbial decomposition consumes oxygen, and low dissolved oxygen can stress or kill aquatic organisms.

questions.prompt: Which wastewater-treatment step primarily uses microorganisms to break down dissolved organic matter?
choices: Screening in preliminary treatment
Primary sedimentation only
Secondary treatment
Chlorine disinfection only
questions.explanation: Secondary treatment uses biological processes, often microbes, to reduce biodegradable organic matter. Primary treatment removes settleable solids; advanced treatment can remove nutrients or contaminants.

questions.prompt: A power plant releases warmed cooling water into a stream. Which effect is most likely downstream?
choices: Warmer water holds more dissolved oxygen and lowers the metabolic demand of fish
Temperature changes affect only water density, not organisms
All aquatic species have identical temperature tolerances
Warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen and can increase metabolic demand
questions.explanation: Warm water holds less oxygen, and temperature also affects metabolism and species distributions. Effects depend on the magnitude and timing of warming and local conditions.

questions.prompt: A response log states: “Skimmers recovered surface oil, while dispersant use reduced slick size but increased oil in the water column.” Which decision approach best evaluates the response?
choices: Compare oil recovery, toxicity, habitat sensitivity, and where dispersed oil may move
Use dispersants whenever a slick shrinks, without monitoring water-column effects
Choose skimming in every case, regardless of waves or habitat access
End response once surface oil is less visible
questions.explanation: The log describes trade-offs. Dispersants can reduce surface slicks but move oil into the water column; skimming can recover oil but depends on sea conditions and may disturb habitat.

questions.prompt: A city bans some single-use plastic bags. Which additional action most directly addresses plastic entering a river from storm drains?
choices: Rely on beach cleanups after plastic has moved downstream
Capture litter at storm drains and improve collection before plastic reaches waterways
Replace bags with a different single-use item that is not collected
Assume that all plastic entering rivers breaks down rapidly into harmless compounds
questions.explanation: Preventing litter and capturing trash before it enters waterways can reduce plastic inputs. Product redesign, reuse systems, collection, and disposal also matter.

questions.prompt: A persistent pollutant has concentrations of 0.02 ppm in plankton, 0.2 ppm in small fish, 1.5 ppm in large fish, and 4.0 ppm in fish-eating birds. Which pattern is shown?
choices: Biodegradation by microbes in the water
Dilution as the pollutant moves to higher trophic levels
Biomagnification across trophic levels
Nutrient cycling
questions.explanation: Concentration increases from plankton to top consumers, demonstrating biomagnification. Persistent pollutants can become more concentrated in organisms at higher trophic levels.

questions.prompt: In a controlled toxicity study with the same test species and exposure period, Substance X has an LD₅₀ of 5 mg/kg and Substance Y has an LD₅₀ of 50 mg/kg. What does this suggest?
choices: Y is ten times more acutely toxic than X in this test
Both have identical acute toxicity overall
The values describe chronic, not acute, effects only
X is more acutely toxic under the tested conditions
questions.explanation: LD₅₀ is the dose that kills 50% of a test population. A lower dose producing the same endpoint indicates greater acute toxicity under those study conditions; it does not describe all risks.

questions.prompt: A team tests whether a constructed wetland removes nitrate from farm runoff. Which design best isolates the wetland’s effect?
choices: Measure nitrate entering and leaving the wetland and compare with a similar untreated channel over the same period
Measure nitrate once downstream after a large storm and compare that single value with a published regional average
Change nitrate input, flow rate and sampling time together during the study, without any untreated comparison channel
Sample a different watershed for each measurement and compare them without matching conditions
questions.explanation: Paired inlet-outlet measurements plus a comparable untreated channel help separate wetland removal from dilution or changing inputs. Repeated sampling and similar flow conditions further strengthen inference.

questions.prompt: Runoff carrying pesticides from many lawns and fields is generally classified as nonpoint-source pollution.
questions.explanation: The pollutant arrives from diffuse areas rather than a single identifiable discharge point.

questions.prompt: A high biochemical oxygen demand usually means microorganisms may consume more dissolved oxygen while decomposing organic matter.
questions.explanation: BOD estimates oxygen use during microbial breakdown of organic matter. High BOD can contribute to oxygen depletion.

questions.prompt: Bioaccumulation describes a chemical becoming more concentrated in organisms at each successive trophic level.
questions.explanation: Bioaccumulation is buildup within an organism over time. Biomagnification is increasing concentration across trophic levels in a food chain.

questions.prompt: What is biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), and what does a high value suggest?
questions.answer: BOD is the amount of dissolved oxygen microorganisms use while decomposing organic matter in a water sample over a defined period. A high value suggests substantial biodegradable organic matter and potential oxygen depletion.
questions.explanation: BOD depends on test conditions such as duration and temperature; report those when comparing measurements.

questions.prompt: What are the main stages of conventional municipal wastewater treatment?
questions.answer: Preliminary treatment screens large debris; primary treatment settles solids; secondary biological treatment removes much biodegradable organic matter; tertiary or advanced treatment can remove nutrients or additional contaminants; disinfection reduces pathogens before discharge or reuse.
questions.explanation: Treatment stages vary by facility and permit; not all plants use the same advanced processes.

questions.prompt: Distinguish bioaccumulation from biomagnification.
questions.answer: Bioaccumulation is a chemical building up in one organism over time when uptake exceeds elimination. Biomagnification is a rise in pollutant concentration across trophic levels in a food chain.
questions.explanation: Persistent substances are more likely to bioaccumulate and biomagnify, though chemical properties and food-web structure matter.

questions.prompt: How does hazardous waste differ from ordinary solid waste, and name one management approach.
questions.answer: Hazardous waste poses risks such as toxicity, corrosivity, reactivity, or ignitability. It may require specialized containment, treatment, tracking, or secure disposal to prevent exposure and environmental release.
questions.explanation: The right management method depends on the waste properties and applicable regulations.

questions.prompt: How can water and sanitation interventions reduce infectious disease, and what limitation should planners consider?
questions.answer: Treating drinking water, safely managing sewage, handwashing, and controlling vectors can interrupt pathogen transmission. Planners must consider infrastructure, maintenance, equitable access, behavior, and the specific transmission route.
