questions.explanation: Some diseases spread through contaminated water; others use vectors, droplets, food, or direct contact, so interventions must match the pathway.

questions.prompt: What is an important consequence of stratospheric ozone depletion?
choices: Less ultraviolet-B radiation reaches the surface, so organisms there receive less exposure
More ultraviolet-B radiation can reach Earth’s surface, increasing exposure for organisms
Ground-level ozone immediately disappears everywhere when stratospheric ozone declines
The effect is limited to human health and does not affect plants, plankton or ecosystems
questions.explanation: Stratospheric ozone absorbs much UV-B radiation. Depletion can increase UV-B reaching the surface, affecting people, plants, and aquatic organisms.

questions.prompt: A science bulletin reports: “After countries phased out many CFC uses under the Montreal Protocol, emissions of ozone-depleting substances fell; recovery of the ozone layer takes time.” Which claim is supported?
choices: The agreement immediately removed ozone-depleting chemicals already in the atmosphere
The agreement primarily phased out carbon dioxide from power plants
Coordinated phaseout reduced a major cause of ozone depletion, but recovery is gradual
The agreement replaced ozone monitoring with climate monitoring
questions.explanation: The bulletin supports a link between the phaseout and lower emissions while recognizing atmospheric persistence and gradual recovery. The treaty targeted ozone-depleting substances.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the natural greenhouse effect?
choices: Greenhouse gases mainly reflect incoming visible sunlight back to space, which cools the upper atmosphere
The ozone layer traps nearly all incoming solar energy close to the surface, warming the ground
Clouds absorb all incoming ultraviolet radiation before it reaches Earth and re-emit it as heat
Atmospheric gases absorb and re-emit outgoing infrared radiation, warming the surface and lower atmosphere
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared energy, warming the lower atmosphere and surface. Human activities increase concentrations of several greenhouse gases and strengthen this effect.

questions.prompt: Which activity is a major human source of carbon dioxide?
choices: Burning coal or petroleum for electricity and transportation
Generating electricity with wind turbines on land and offshore
Photosynthesis in a forest that is recovering after logging
Generating electricity through nuclear fission in reactors
questions.explanation: Combustion of fossil fuels transfers geologic carbon to the atmosphere as CO₂. Deforestation and cement production are also important human sources.

questions.prompt: Corals commonly bleach when stressed by unusually warm water because they:
choices: They convert their calcium carbonate skeleton into oxygen that escapes into the water
They lose or expel symbiotic algae that normally provide much of their energy
They develop their own chlorophyll to replace the symbiotic algae they normally host
They stop exchanging dissolved substances with the seawater around their tissues
questions.explanation: Heat stress can disrupt the coral-algae relationship, causing corals to lose symbiotic algae and appear white. Bleaching can be reversible if conditions improve, but prolonged stress can cause mortality.

questions.prompt: Which action is an example of climate adaptation?
choices: Replacing coal-fired generation with new wind power
Capturing carbon dioxide from a power plant smokestack
Raising critical equipment above projected flood levels
Reducing methane leakage from natural gas pipelines
questions.explanation: Adaptation adjusts systems to reduce harm from climate impacts. The other options reduce greenhouse-gas emissions and are mitigation measures.

questions.prompt: A study reports annual mean temperature anomalies of 0.2°C in 1990, 0.5°C in 2000, 0.8°C in 2010, and 1.1°C in 2020 relative to the same baseline. What trend is supported?
choices: The mean anomaly across the four observations was exactly 0.5°C above baseline
The anomaly increased by 0.9°C in each decade between 1990 and 2020
The data establish an identical warming trend at every location on Earth
The anomaly increased by about 0.3°C per decade in these observations
questions.explanation: Each decade increases by 0.3°C in the supplied values. This is a trend in the stated dataset, not proof that every location changes at the same rate.

questions.prompt: A coastal gauge records sea level relative to land rising from 0 cm to 6 cm over 20 years. What is the average rate of relative sea-level rise?
choices: 0.03 cm/year
0.3 cm/year
3 cm/year
12 cm/year
questions.explanation: Average rate = change / time = 6 cm / 20 years = 0.3 cm/year. Relative sea level also reflects local land movement, not only ocean volume.

questions.prompt: As more atmospheric CO₂ dissolves in seawater, which chemical change contributes to lower ocean pH?
choices: More hydrogen ions are released, lowering pH and reducing carbonate availability
Hydrogen-ion concentration declines, raising pH and reducing carbonate availability
Seawater pH rises because carbonic acid is a base
Dissolved CO₂ removes all calcium ions from seawater
questions.explanation: Dissolved CO₂ reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which can release hydrogen ions and lower pH. This reduces carbonate ion availability for some shell-building organisms.

questions.prompt: As Arctic sea ice melts, darker ocean water absorbs more solar energy than reflective ice. What type of feedback can this create?
choices: Negative feedback that counteracts the initial warming
No feedback because melting ice does not change reflectivity
Positive feedback that amplifies initial warming
A feedback that changes ocean salinity but not energy absorption
questions.explanation: Lower albedo means more solar energy is absorbed, contributing to additional warming and ice melt. The loop amplifies the initial change, so it is a positive feedback.

questions.prompt: A mountain species is observed at progressively higher elevations during warmer decades, while suitable habitat shrinks near the summit. Which risk is most directly suggested?
choices: Unlimited expansion of its range as the climate continues to warm
No relationship between temperature and the species' distribution
Reduced extinction risk for every species living on the mountain slopes
Habitat loss as the species runs out of cooler high-elevation area
questions.explanation: Some species shift ranges as climate changes, but mountaintop species may lose habitat because they cannot move higher indefinitely. Dispersal barriers and other stressors also matter.

questions.prompt: A nonnative plant spreads rapidly along a road corridor, displacing native plants and changing fire frequency. Which response is most likely to be effective?
choices: Combine early detection, targeted removal, prevention of seed spread, and follow-up monitoring
Wait until the species is widespread along the corridor before assessing any control options
Apply the same broad-spectrum herbicide across all habitats along the road at the same time
Remove the native vegetation first, then monitor only the invasive plant for later spread
questions.explanation: Invasive-species management often works best when detected early and paired with targeted control and monitoring. Methods should account for non-target species, cost, and reinvasion risk.

questions.prompt: A highway divides two habitat patches used by a wide-ranging mammal. Which design may improve movement while maintaining nearby development?
choices: A crossing placed far from any habitat, with no cover on either approach
A wildlife crossing placed along a movement route and linked to suitable habitat
More fencing, with no crossing, at the places where animals already try to cross
A narrow vegetated strip that leads animals up to the highway barrier and ends there
questions.explanation: Corridors and wildlife crossings can reconnect fragmented habitat and support movement. Their success depends on placement, species behavior, maintenance, and road-safety design.

questions.prompt: An analyst writes: “Because greenhouse gases mix in the atmosphere, a country’s emissions affect people beyond its borders.” Which rationale for international agreements does this statement support?
choices: Countries can use agreements to stop greenhouse gases from crossing national borders
An agreement automatically enforces every national target it contains
Countries can coordinate reductions and assistance for a shared global problem
International agreements remove all economic trade-offs between countries
questions.explanation: The statement supports collective action because emissions have cross-border effects. Agreements can coordinate goals and support, although participation and implementation vary.

questions.prompt: A transit agency report states: “New electric buses use electricity from a lower-carbon grid mix than the diesel buses they replaced.” Which climate benefit is intended?
choices: Reduce tailpipe emissions of nitrogen oxides and particulate matter
Reduce fuel use per passenger trip
Reduce traffic noise along the bus route
Reduce lifecycle greenhouse-gas emissions from transportation
questions.explanation: Using lower-carbon electricity can reduce lifecycle greenhouse-gas emissions from transport. Battery production, electricity generation, and vehicle use still have environmental impacts.

questions.prompt: Researchers test whether elevated seawater temperature increases coral bleaching. Which design best supports a causal conclusion?
choices: Randomly assign similar coral fragments to replicated control and warmer tanks with other conditions held constant
Compare one naturally warm reef with one different cooler reef and assume temperature is the only difference between them
Change temperature, pH, light, and salinity together in one tank and measure how much the corals bleach afterward
Measure bleaching only once at the end of the experiment, without a baseline or an untreated comparison group
questions.explanation: Replicated randomized treatments, controlled conditions, and a measured bleaching response help isolate the temperature effect. A laboratory study may not capture all reef conditions or long-term processes.

questions.prompt: A campus emits 400 metric tons of CO₂-equivalent per year. An efficiency project is expected to reduce emissions by 15%. What annual emissions remain?
choices: 60 metric tons CO₂e
340 metric tons CO₂e
385 metric tons CO₂e
460 metric tons CO₂e
questions.explanation: Reduction = 400 × 0.15 = 60 metric tons CO₂e. Remaining emissions = 400 − 60 = 340 metric tons CO₂e/year.

questions.prompt: A small endemic frog population occupies one wetland that is being drained and also faces a newly introduced pathogen. Why is extinction risk especially high?
choices: Its large range makes it vulnerable only to competition from other frogs in the same wetland
The pathogen increases population size by reducing competition among the surviving frogs
Its narrow range and small population make it vulnerable to habitat loss and disease
Wetland protection guarantees the population cannot become extinct
questions.explanation: A narrow range and small population increase vulnerability to habitat change and stochastic events. Multiple stressors can interact and reduce recovery options.

questions.prompt: A marine heat wave raises water temperature for several weeks. Which combination of effects is plausible?
choices: Higher temperature guarantees greater dissolved oxygen at every depth
A brief heat wave reverses ocean acidification globally
Ocean thermal inertia prevents organisms from responding
Heat stress may cause bleaching and shifts in species distributions
questions.explanation: Marine heat waves can stress organisms, contribute to bleaching, and shift distributions. Ocean thermal inertia slows some changes but does not prevent ecological responses.

questions.prompt: A conservation plan protects a large reserve but ignores the surrounding agricultural landscape. Which addition may improve persistence for wide-ranging species?
choices: Add habitat connections and wildlife-friendly practices beyond the reserve boundary
Remove buffer habitat around the reserve to reduce the total length of habitat edge
Increase the reserve's isolation so that no species can move in or out across its boundary
Focus only on visitor access while leaving habitat links unchanged
questions.explanation: Protected areas are important, but connectivity, buffer zones, land-use practices, and community engagement can support movement and reduce edge pressures.

questions.prompt: A coastal city compares a seawall and restored wetlands for flood risk. The wall protects dense infrastructure but may shift erosion; wetlands can store surge water and support habitat but need space and time to establish. What is the strongest recommendation?
choices: Choose the seawall, because a hard structure removes all future flood risk for the protected area and needs no review
Compare site-specific flood projections, costs, habitat, maintenance, equity, and hybrid options before selecting measures
Choose wetlands, because natural defenses need no land, maintenance or time to become effective against storm surge
Reject both options, because local flooding depends only on rainfall and not on sea level rise
questions.explanation: Both measures have benefits and limitations. A defensible plan uses local evidence, considers who is protected or displaced, and may combine gray and nature-based approaches.

questions.prompt: The greenhouse effect is a natural process, and rising greenhouse-gas concentrations from human activities can strengthen it.
questions.explanation: The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warmer than it would otherwise be; anthropogenic increases in greenhouse gases add radiative forcing.

questions.prompt: Ocean acidification means ocean pH is decreasing; it does not mean seawater has become acidic everywhere.
questions.explanation: Ocean pH has declined relative to preindustrial conditions, but average seawater remains slightly alkaline. Local conditions vary.

questions.prompt: Mitigation reduces the causes of climate change, while adaptation reduces harm from climate impacts.
questions.explanation: Emissions reduction and carbon removal are mitigation; flood defenses and heat-health plans are adaptation. Some actions can support both.

questions.prompt: Every nonnative species becomes invasive and harms every ecosystem it enters.
questions.explanation: Many nonnative species do not become invasive. Impacts depend on species traits, ecosystem context, and interactions; invasive species are those that spread and cause harm.

questions.prompt: A positive climate feedback amplifies an initial climate change, while a negative feedback counteracts it.
questions.explanation: Positive and negative describe the direction of the feedback effect, not whether the effect is beneficial or harmful to people.

questions.prompt: Distinguish climate mitigation from climate adaptation and give one example of each.
questions.answer: Mitigation reduces greenhouse-gas emissions or increases removals, such as clean electricity or forest restoration. Adaptation reduces harm from impacts, such as heat-health plans or flood-resilient infrastructure.
questions.explanation: Some actions provide both benefits, but classify them by their primary purpose.

questions.prompt: How do CFCs deplete stratospheric ozone, and what did the Montreal Protocol do?
questions.answer: UV radiation breaks down CFCs and releases chlorine that catalytically destroys ozone. The Montreal Protocol coordinated a phaseout of ozone-depleting substances.
questions.explanation: The treaty addresses stratospheric ozone depletion; it is distinct from climate agreements focused on greenhouse gases.

questions.prompt: Name four important greenhouse gases and one major human source for each.
questions.answer: Carbon dioxide: fossil-fuel combustion or deforestation; methane: fossil-fuel systems, livestock, or landfills; nitrous oxide: fertilized soils and some industrial processes; fluorinated gases: refrigeration and industrial uses.
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases differ in atmospheric lifetime and heat-trapping strength. Water vapor is also a greenhouse gas but is primarily a feedback in climate discussions.

questions.prompt: Name two major contributors to global mean sea-level rise and one reason local relative sea level may differ.
questions.answer: Warming causes seawater thermal expansion and melting land ice adds water to oceans. Local relative sea level also depends on land subsidence or uplift, currents, and gravity-related effects.
questions.explanation: Sea-level rise is not spatially uniform; local planning should use relative sea-level projections.

questions.prompt: Explain how rising atmospheric CO₂ can affect shell-building marine organisms.
questions.answer: More CO₂ dissolves into seawater, forming carbonic acid and increasing hydrogen ions. This reduces carbonate ion availability, which can make it harder for some organisms to build or maintain calcium carbonate shells.
questions.explanation: Organism responses vary by species and can also be influenced by temperature, food, and local chemistry.

questions.prompt: Describe the ice-albedo feedback as a cause-and-effect loop.
questions.answer: Initial warming melts reflective snow or ice; darker land or ocean is exposed and absorbs more solar energy; added absorption causes further warming and additional melting.
questions.explanation: This is a positive feedback because it amplifies the initial change.

questions.prompt: Compare in situ and ex situ conservation.
questions.answer: In situ conservation protects species in their natural habitats through reserves, habitat restoration, and connectivity. Ex situ conservation protects organisms outside their habitats, such as in seed banks, botanical gardens, or captive-breeding programs.
questions.explanation: Ex situ methods can serve as a backup but do not preserve all ecological interactions or solve habitat loss on their own.

questions.prompt: Name one benefit and one limitation of international environmental agreements.
questions.answer: Agreements can coordinate shared goals, monitoring, funding, and action across borders. Limits include uneven participation, national implementation, enforcement, costs, and differences in responsibility or capacity.
questions.explanation: The Montreal Protocol demonstrates coordinated action on ozone-depleting substances; climate agreements face different sources and economic trade-offs.

questions.prompt: How should a student evaluate a claim that a climate trend in one region proves the global climate is changing?
questions.answer: Check the time span, measurement methods, baseline, uncertainty, and whether the data represent one location or a global dataset. Compare multiple independent observations and distinguish short-term variability from long-term trends.
questions.explanation: A single regional record can be evidence about that region but cannot alone establish a global trend or attribute its cause.
